lessons.title: Nature as One Connected System
body: Environmental science begins with the idea that nature is connected. Alexander von Humboldt, travelling through the Americas around 1800, noticed that climate, altitude and vegetation line up in belts, and that cutting forests changes local climate. He treated nature as a single web rather than a list of separate species.

In 1935 the botanist Arthur Tansley coined the word ecosystem for a community of organisms together with the physical environment they interact with. Eugene Odum later made the ecosystem the central unit of ecology and studied how energy flows and nutrients cycle through it. Vladimir Vernadsky took a still wider view. He described the biosphere as the thin global zone of life, and argued that life is a geological force that shapes the atmosphere, oceans and rocks.

A simple example is a pond. Its water chemistry, sunlight, algae, insects, fish and bacteria all affect each other. If you change one part, such as adding fertiliser, the effects spread to the others. Seeing these links is the foundation for understanding climate, pollution and conservation.

lessons.title: Energy Flow and Food Webs
body: Almost all ecosystems run on sunlight. Producers such as plants and algae capture it by photosynthesis. Herbivores eat the producers, carnivores eat the herbivores, and decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil and water. Each feeding stage is a trophic level.

Energy is lost at every step, mostly as heat from the organisms' own metabolism. Only about 10 percent is passed on to the next level, so roughly 90 percent is lost. If grass fixes 10 000 kilojoules of energy, herbivores might hold about 1000 and carnivores about 100. This is why food chains are short, and why there are fewer top predators than prey. Raymond Lindeman's 1942 work quantified these energy transfers.

Nutrients behave differently from energy: atoms of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus are recycled by decomposers rather than lost. Top predators can have a large influence on the whole system. When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, elk behaviour and numbers changed, vegetation recovered along streams, and even rivers were affected. This chain of effects is called a trophic cascade.

lessons.title: Population Growth and Limits
body: A population with unlimited resources grows exponentially, but resources are never unlimited. The logistic model describes this: dN/dt = r N (1 - N / K). N is the population size, r is the intrinsic growth rate and K is the carrying capacity, the number the environment can sustain. When N is small, growth is almost exponential. As N approaches K the factor (1 - N / K) shrinks toward zero and growth stops. If N is above K the population declines.
Suppose r = 0.5 per year, K = 1000 and N = 500. Then dN/dt = 0.5 times 500 times (1 - 0.5) = 125 individuals per year. Growth is fastest at about half the carrying capacity.

A related idea applies to the spread of an infection or an invasive species. In the SIR model, individuals are susceptible, infected or recovered. The basic reproduction number is R0 = beta / gamma, where beta is the transmission rate and gamma is the recovery rate. If R0 is above 1 an outbreak grows, and if it is below 1 it dies out. With beta = 0.6 and gamma = 0.2, R0 = 3.

lessons.title: Discovering the Greenhouse Effect
body: Earth's average surface temperature is about plus 15 degrees Celsius. Without any greenhouse gases, the same sunlight would leave it near minus 18. The difference is the greenhouse effect. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface, which gives off infrared radiation. Gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane absorb that infrared and re-emit it in all directions, sending part of it back down.

The science was worked out step by step. In 1856 Eunice Newton Foote showed that a jar of carbon dioxide in sunlight heated more and cooled more slowly than ordinary air. In 1859 John Tyndall measured precisely how much infrared radiation water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb. In 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated by hand how much the surface would warm if carbon dioxide levels changed, and linked fossil fuel burning to future warming.

Greenhouse gases are essential to life, as a planet without them would be frozen. The concern today is that people are adding to them. Later satellite measurements, such as those reported by Harries and colleagues in 2001, directly observed the greenhouse fingerprint in the radiation escaping to space growing stronger.

lessons.title: Earth's Energy Balance
body: Every warm object radiates energy. The Stefan-Boltzmann law says the power radiated per square metre is j = sigma T to the fourth power, where T is the absolute temperature in kelvin and sigma is a constant. Because of the fourth power, a small rise in temperature produces a large rise in radiated energy. If the absolute temperature doubles, the radiated power increases by 2 to the fourth, or 16 times.

A planet reaches balance when it radiates as much energy as it absorbs. Absorbed energy depends on the sunlight S and the albedo, the fraction reflected by clouds, ice and the surface. The equilibrium temperature, T = [S (1 - albedo) / (4 sigma)] to the power 1/4, is the temperature without greenhouse gases. Ice and clouds with high albedo reflect sunlight and cool the planet, while dark oceans and forests absorb more.

This explains an important feedback. When ice melts, darker water or land is exposed, albedo falls, more sunlight is absorbed, and warming increases. Greenhouse gases do not change the incoming sunlight but alter how easily infrared escapes. Adding carbon dioxide raises the height from which the planet effectively radiates to space, so the surface below must warm to restore balance.

lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle
body: Carbon moves among four great reservoirs: the atmosphere, the ocean, the land biosphere and rock. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air and respiration returns it, which creates the seasonal sawtooth in the Keeling Curve, the continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide that Charles Keeling began at Mauna Loa in 1958. A much slower geological loop of volcanism, weathering and burial operates over millions of years.

The key issue is rate. Fossil fuels are the remains of plants buried over hundreds of millions of years. Burning them moves that carbon into the atmosphere within decades, much faster than weathering and ocean uptake can remove it. About half of emitted carbon dioxide stays in the air, and the ocean takes up much of the rest.

We know the extra carbon dioxide is from fossil fuels from several lines of evidence. The Keeling Curve shows the steady rise, and ice cores show present levels are far above the range of the last 800 000 years. The Suess effect, a fall in the carbon-13 to carbon-12 ratio in air, fits carbon from ancient plants, because plants favour the lighter isotope.

lessons.title: Radiative Forcing and Climate Change
body: Radiative forcing is the change in Earth's energy balance caused by some factor, measured in watts per square metre. For carbon dioxide it is given by delta F = 5.35 ln(C / C0), where C is the new concentration and C0 the reference. Because the relationship is logarithmic, each doubling of carbon dioxide adds about the same forcing, roughly 3.7 watts per square metre, no matter where you start.

The global surface has warmed by more than 1 degree Celsius since pre-industrial times. The evidence is consistent across independent datasets such as GISTEMP and HadCRUT, and the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report concludes that warming is unequivocal and caused by human activity. Fingerprints help identify the cause: nights are warming faster than days, and the lower atmosphere warms while the stratosphere cools. That pattern matches greenhouse gases rather than a brighter Sun, which would warm both.

Warming has other consequences. The Clausius-Clapeyron relation shows that the air can hold about 7 percent more water vapour for each degree Celsius of warming. This intensifies heavy rainfall, and in other regions faster evaporation worsens drought. Past episodes such as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum show how carbon-driven warming has affected the planet before.

lessons.title: Ocean Acidification
body: The ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of the carbon dioxide people have emitted. Henry's law explains why: the concentration of a dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure, C = kH p. More carbon dioxide in the air means more dissolves in the sea. There it reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions.

Acidity is measured on the pH scale, pH = minus log10 of the hydrogen ion concentration. The scale is logarithmic, so a drop of 1 pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration is 10 times higher. The surface ocean has already dropped by about 0.1 pH units since pre-industrial times, which corresponds to roughly a 30 percent increase in acidity. Ocean time-series stations such as Station ALOHA show the decline tracking the rise in carbon dioxide.

The ocean is not becoming acidic in the sense of being below pH 7; it is becoming less alkaline. The key concern is biological. The extra hydrogen ions reduce the carbonate ions that corals, shellfish and some plankton need to build calcium carbonate skeletons and shells. Laboratory and field experiments show slower calcification in high-CO2 seawater, which threatens marine food webs.

lessons.title: The Ozone Layer
body: A layer of ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, protecting living things from damage to cells and DNA. It is a different issue from the greenhouse effect: ozone depletion concerns the thinning of this shield, not the warming of the climate.

In the 1970s Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, working with ideas from Paul Crutzen's ozone chemistry, showed that chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays, are stable enough to drift up to the stratosphere. There, ultraviolet light breaks them apart and the released chlorine destroys ozone in catalytic reactions, so one chlorine atom can destroy many ozone molecules. James Lovelock's electron capture detector had revealed that CFCs were spreading worldwide.

In 1985 scientists reported the Antarctic ozone hole. Two years later, in 1987, countries agreed the Montreal Protocol to phase out CFCs. It is widely regarded as one of the most successful environmental treaties, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering. It shows that when scientific evidence is clear and alternatives exist, global cooperation can work.

lessons.title: Water and Nitrogen Cycles
body: The water cycle moves water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and groundwater. It is driven by the Sun and links the ocean, atmosphere and land, and it redistributes heat as water evaporates in one place and condenses in another.

Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but most organisms cannot use it directly. Certain microbes and lightning convert it into forms such as ammonia and nitrate in a process called fixation. Plants absorb these, animals eat plants, decomposers return nitrogen to the soil, and other bacteria eventually convert it back to nitrogen gas.

In the early 1900s people learned to make fertiliser industrially, and this approximately doubled the natural flow of fixed nitrogen on land. Much of the excess runs off fields into rivers and coasts. There, it feeds explosive algal growth, and when the algae die, bacteria use up the oxygen in the water as they decompose them. The result is low-oxygen dead zones where fish cannot live. The Hubbard Brook study showed in a whole watershed how disturbing a forest disrupts nutrient cycling. Nutrient flows are one of the planetary boundaries that scientists track.

lessons.title: Biodiversity and Habitat Loss
body: Biodiversity is the variety of life at three levels: genetic variation within a species, the number of species in a community, and the range of ecosystems across a landscape. It matters because diverse ecosystems are more productive and more stable. Long-term plots at Cedar Creek showed that more diverse plots produce more and recover better from drought, since if one species struggles, another can take over its role.

The species-area relationship says that the number of species rises with habitat area according to S = c A to the power z. Suppose z = 0.5. If a forest loses three quarters of its area, so A falls to one quarter, then the number of species falls to 0.25 to the power 0.5, which is one half. Ecologists use this relationship to estimate how many species will be lost when habitat shrinks. The island biogeography work of MacArthur and Wilson also underpins how reserves are designed.

The main drivers of current losses are habitat loss, climate change, overexploitation and invasive species. The IPBES assessment in 2019 estimated that around one million species face extinction, and the IUCN Red List tracks the status of species. Extinction rates are now far above the natural background rate.

lessons.title: The Conservation Movement
body: Scientific understanding became a movement through people who could persuade the public. John Muir campaigned to protect Yosemite and the Sierra, co-founded the Sierra Club, and helped build support for the national park system. Aldo Leopold, a wildlife ecologist, wrote A Sand County Almanac and set out the land ethic: humans should see themselves as members of the ecological community, not as its conquerors.

In 1962 Rachel Carson published Silent Spring. It documented how synthetic pesticides such as DDT spread through food webs and harm birds and other wildlife. She explained bioaccumulation, in which a persistent chemical becomes more concentrated at each step up the food chain, so that predators carry the highest loads. The book awakened the modern environmental movement and led to tighter regulation of pesticides. The first Earth Day followed in 1970.

Wangari Maathai of Kenya founded the Green Belt Movement, which has planted tens of millions of trees. She linked restoring the environment with women's rights and democracy, and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. These figures show that environmental protection involves ethics, politics and communities as well as science.

lessons.title: Planetary Boundaries and the Anthropocene
body: In 2000 the atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen proposed the name Anthropocene for a proposed geological epoch in which human activity has become the dominant force shaping Earth's climate and ecosystems. The idea reflects measurable changes: altered carbon and nitrogen cycles, a warming climate, and widespread extinctions.

In 2009 Johan Rockstrom and colleagues introduced the planetary boundaries framework. It identifies nine Earth-system processes that together keep the planet in the stable, Holocene-like state in which agriculture and civilisation developed. These include climate change, biosphere integrity, nutrient flows of nitrogen and phosphorus, land-system change, freshwater use, ocean acidification and novel entities such as synthetic chemicals. For each, the framework proposes a boundary beyond which the risk of abrupt, large-scale change rises sharply. Staying inside all of them defines a safe operating space for humanity.

The framework has been updated twice, in 2015 and 2023. The 2023 assessment by Richardson and colleagues concluded that six of the nine boundaries had been transgressed. A boundary is not a cliff edge but a zone of growing risk. The framework helps connect separate problems such as climate, biodiversity and pollution into a single picture of planetary health, and it frames the goals of agreements such as the Paris Agreement of 2015.
